title: Celestica Q3 2026: A $40B Guide, Priced As If Growth Ends In 2027
description: Revenue +83%, a first 2027 outlook of $40B, and a FCF cut to pay for it. Keeping BUY, target trimmed to $560 from $575.
body_html:
In August, Celestica [] sold 11.1M new shares at $310 to fund its next leg of growth. On October 27 it told you what that leg looks like: $40B of revenue in 2027, +90% on this year, and adjusted EPS of $21.50. As I write this, the same shares cost $258, 17% below what the new shareholders paid less than three months ago.

The fall came before the print. CLS closed at $388 on October 6 and at $247 on October 26, the day it reported. The worst session was October 22, when it lost 12% in a broad risk-off day for AI hardware with no company news behind it. The results added 12% the next morning and 8% the day after. By Friday, Mr. Market had taken most of it back.

It’s the fourth markdown like this in 2026. On January 22, CLS lost as much as 12% in a session on a misread DigiTimes report. After the Q4 2025 print it fell from $340 to $295…

… and after Q1 2026 from $420 to $355, both times on results that beat and raised the year.

The 2026 revenue guide went up after every one of them, from $16B to $21B.

CLS was among the first positions I added when I started this newsletter, and I have held it since 2023. I published the deep dive in April 2025 with a $153 target.

This is my fourth update this year; the last was my Q2 2026 review in July.

The tracker shows the TSX-listed shares in Canadian dollars, which is where I hold the position.

Everything below is in US dollars on the NYSE line. The weight is down from 8.3% in July because the price fell. I haven’t bought or sold.

This post is free. If someone you know sold CLS in October because the chart looked broken, send them the section on what $258 implies.

Table of Contents

  • TLDR

  • How CLS ranks

  • Q3 2026: what the print said

  • Cash, working capital and the balance sheet

  • Guidance: what changed in 90 days

  • Thesis scorecard after Q3 2026

  • Valuation: why the target moves to $560

  • What $258 implies

  • Risk register

  • Verdict

TLDR

  • Q3 revenue grew 83% y/y and adjusted EPS grew 109%, both above the top of the guide. Adjusted operating margin set another record.

  • The first 2027 outlook calls for revenue +90% and adjusted EPS +86%, 18% and 15% above the floors management implied in July.

  • The 2026 FCF guide fell 23%, and 2027 turns cash-negative as inventory and capex fund the ramp.

  • The three largest customers made up 66% of revenue, up from 59% a year ago.

  • Five of six thesis pillars are confirmed and strengthening. Capital returns moves to challenged.

  • At $258, the price assumes revenue stops growing after 2027 and stays there for a decade.

  • Keeping BUY. Target trimmed to $560 from $575, against a $150 bear case.

How CLS ranks

The RS score is 62, ten points lower than in July. Sentiment fell from 53 and Outlook from 85, while Valuation rose from 20 as the price came down.

Sentiment 25. It’s the lowest score in the peer table below, after the share price lost a third in three weeks.

Growth 93. The weak spots are the forward EBITDA and EPS growth metrics. Forward EPS growth of 59% sits well below the 86% CLS guided for 2027. If estimates move toward the guide, this score moves with them.

Profitability 79. This is the business model in one table. Returns on capital score near the top and gross margin scores near the bottom, because CLS earns a thin spread on hardware that turns over fast. The levered FCF margin is low for the reason covered in the cash section below: the company is pouring cash into inventory and capacity.

Valuation 38. Price to cash flow carries the inventory build in its denominator, and EV to invested capital is high because the returns on that capital are high. The PEG ratio and forward EV to sales score well. On the 2027 guide, CLS trades at 12x adjusted EPS.

Flex [] carries a market value close to CLS’s and grows forward revenue at half the rate on a lower EBIT margin. Jabil [] is smaller and grows at a third of the rate. Sanmina [] matches the growth score on a margin below 6%. CLS has the fastest forward revenue growth in the group and the lowest sentiment score.

Q3 2026: what the print said

Revenue grew 83% y/y and beat consensus by 8%.

Adjusted EPS grew 109% and beat by 13%.

Both lines cleared the top of the range by a wide margin. Revenue landed 5% above the top of the guide and adjusted EPS 7% above it. That’s the fifth quarter in a row above the top of the EPS range. GAAP EPS grew 41%, held back by a $113M mark-to-market gain on the company’s share swap that flattered Q3 2025.

The margin story kept going. Adjusted operating margin set another record, while adjusted gross margin slipped 50bps to 11.2% on mix. The mix shift is Compute & Storage, which carries a lower gross margin than networking and is now the fastest-growing line in the company. Operating leverage more than covered it.

CCS did the work again. It doubled and now accounts for 84% of revenue. Networking beat its own outlook of 60% growth, and Compute & Storage beat 190%. HPS, the design-led business at the centre of the thesis, grew 70% to $2.3B and 40% of revenue.

Compute & Storage is changing the shape of the company. It went from 15% of revenue to 28% in a year. In 2027 it grows faster than networking as Google’s next TPU generation and OpenAI’s Jalapeño system move into volume. That’s why management guides 2027 gross margin in the low 11s even as operating margin rises.

ATS set a record too. Revenue grew 23% against a mid-teens outlook, led by semiconductor capital equipment, and the segment margin is the highest in its history for the second quarter in a row.

Cash, working capital and the balance sheet

FCF was $413M through nine months. Capex ran at 4.7% of revenue in the quarter, against 1.2% a year earlier. The capacity is going into Texas, Monterrey, Thailand, Japan and Malaysia, and into power: CLS is adding hundreds of megawatts across its network so it can take programmes that competitors without the power can’t.

Inventory is where the cash went, and suppliers paid for it. Inventory rose $1.1B in the quarter. Accounts payable rose $1.2B over the same three months, from $3.82B in June to $5.04B in September. A company the supply chain doubts doesn’t get those terms. The same trade credit carries no coupon and no covenant, and it reverses fast if suppliers tighten.

The 2026 FCF guide falls because the build continues into Q4. The $460M full-year number leaves less than $50M for the fourth quarter.

The August raise did its job. Net debt of $274.7M in June became net cash of $3.14B in September after $3.39B of net proceeds.

That cash is the funding for 2027’s working capital. No shares were repurchased in Q3. The TSX has accepted a renewed buyback for up to 2.5% of the float, and shares sold at $310 in August can be bought back at $258 today. Management’s stated priority is organic growth first.

Guidance: what changed in 90 days

2026 got its fourth raise and its first FCF cut. The revenue outlook now sits 31% above the $16B first guided in October 2025, and the EPS outlook 41% above the original $8.20. FCF went the other way. The $460M is below July’s $600M and below the $500M first guided a year ago.

Q4 calls for revenue +76% and adjusted EPS +84% at the midpoints, on an 8.7% adjusted operating margin.

2027: the operating line keeps July’s promise, and EPS doesn’t. In July management said 2027 EPS would grow faster than revenue. The guide has EPS +86% against revenue +90%. The promise held one line higher. Adjusted operating earnings go from $1.76B to $3.6B, +104%, on a margin of 9%. Two things take it back between operating profit and EPS. The August share sale lifts the diluted count to 127M from 120M this year, and the tax rate rises to 21% from 18% in Q3.

What drives the $40B:

  • CCS grows 110% and ATS 10%, with revenue weighted to the second half.

  • 1.6T switch revenue passes 800G next year while 800G keeps growing.

  • Compute & Storage outgrows networking as the next TPU generation and Jalapeño reach mass production.

  • Capex of $1.5B-$2B is tied to programmes already won, and it covers capacity for 2028 as well.

2028 is already bigger on paper. The company says customer demand forecasts for 2028, built from awarded programmes alone, are “meaningfully higher” than the 2027 outlook. Some of those awards are for silicon that hasn’t been developed yet, and the planning conversations now reach 2029 and 2030. FCF turns positive again in 2028.

Read this team’s revenue and EPS guide as a floor, and its FCF guide as a variable. Five quarters in a row above the top of the EPS range, and four raises to the 2026 revenue outlook. FCF went from $500M to $600M to $460M in twelve months. The cash line moves with the size of the ramp, and the ramp keeps getting bigger.

Thesis scorecard after Q3 2026

Pillar #1. From commodity EMS to AI-infrastructure design partner: confirmed and strengthening

HPS grew 70% and is close to half of CCS revenue. The HPS engineering team goes from 1,600 to more than 2,000 next year. R&D was $78M in 2024, the year before my deep dive, and passes $300M in 2027. Two products from this quarter show where the design work has moved. The DS6010, built with AMD [] for its Helios rack, is the industry’s first 204.8Tb switch, two Tomahawk 6 chips in one chassis, and it ramps by year-end. The DS6005 is CLS’s first co-packaged optics switch, and the company is one of the first to bring up a working platform on Broadcom’s Tomahawk 6 Davisson silicon.

Jalapeño is the bigger proof. CLS co-designed the full inference system around Jalapeño, the custom accelerator OpenAI developed with Broadcom []: a dual-rack unit holding 128 accelerators, a scale-up fabric linking up to 2,048 of them over 1.6T switches, and a custom build of the SONiC network software. The design scope moved from the switch to the whole rack this year.

Pillar #2. Hyperscaler AI infrastructure spend is structural: confirmed and strengthening

The largest AI spenders are on track for $803B-$828B of capex in 2026. Alphabet [] expects its capex to “increase significantly in 2027”, and Amazon [] plans to spend “meaningfully more”. Broadcom has secured supply to double AI semiconductor revenue to $115B in FY2027 and has line of sight to double it again to $230B in FY2028.

CLS’s own read matches. The binding constraint is supply (components, land, power) rather than demand, and the 2028 forecasts on awarded programmes sit above 2027.

In Weekly #104 I named hyperscaler capex guidance as one of three numbers that would change my mind, with a cut as the signal that the cycle is turning. Alphabet and Amazon pointed theirs higher instead.

Pillar #3. The 400G / 800G / 1.6T networking ramp: confirmed and strengthening

Networking grew 68% in Q3 and reaches $11.8B in 2026, +66%. CLS has won ten 1.6T programmes, four of them scale-up and six scale-out. When I wrote about its 800G edge in September 2025, it had won two.

Scale-up is the new piece. Ethernet is moving inside the rack to connect accelerators to each other, a job that used to belong to proprietary links. Dell’Oro expects AI back-end switch sales to approach $1T over 2026-2030, with scale-up passing half the market by 2030 and Ethernet leading it.

CLS starts that cycle from the front. On the data it presented at its October 27 investor day, it holds 31% of 800G-and-above data-centre switching revenue and 58% of custom Ethernet switch revenue, more than double the next supplier. Pluggable optics stay the norm through 1.6T, and co-packaged optics take a larger role at 3.2T. The 1.6T cycle should be bigger than 800G because scale-up adds a second network to every rack.

Pillar #4. Inference-driven durability beyond 2026: confirmed and strengthening

Compute & Storage grew 242% in Q3 and reaches $5.6B in 2026, +170%. The two programmes that carry it into 2027 have names. The first is the next generation of Google’s TPU, on a relationship that already spans several generations. The second is OpenAI’s Jalapeño, its first custom inference accelerator, co-developed with Broadcom, which CLS ramps in the second half of 2027 with successor generations already in development.

The TPU line has a second engine behind it. Broadcom expects Anthropic to become its largest custom-accelerator customer in 2027, and Anthropic’s S-1 shows about $161B of TPU system leases from Broadcom over five-year terms.

The filing never names Celestica. Those leases pay for TPU racks and the networking around them, which is what CLS builds for Google.

In December I argued that the GPU vs. TPU debate is a distraction because CLS builds for both.

The same filing lists more than $20B of AMD Helios racks from 2027 next to the TPU leases, and CLS builds the scale-up switch for every Helios rack.

Pillar #5. FCF machine and capital returns: challenged, by choice

I graded this pillar confirmed and evolving in April and July, when rising capex was the only pressure on it. This quarter the 2026 FCF guide fell to $460M from $600M, and the 2027 guide is a net use of cash. In August the company issued 11.1M shares at $310, adding 9.7% to the share count, and it bought back nothing in Q3.

The pillar as I wrote it promised cash coming back to shareholders. The next fifteen months deliver cash going into inventory and factories, plus new shares. I grade it challenged and I agree with the choice: adjusted ROIC was 64.7% in Q3, and capital that earns that on programmes customers have already awarded is worth more inside the company than in a buyback.

In July I said to watch the October capex number, and that anything well above $1.5B would mean bigger 2028 demand and more pressure on FCF. It came in at $1.5B-$2B, tied to capacity for 2028. What would change my mind is 2027 capex at the top of the range without a matching step-up in the 2028 revenue outlook.

Where we were vs. where we are: in January I set the $575 target with the stock at $280. In July it was $342. Today it is $258, against a $560 target and a $150 bear case.

Pillar #6. Defensive moat via design complexity: confirmed and strengthening

Fewer competitors bid on 800G and 1.6T programmes than on earlier generations, and CLS is winning programmes its competitors can’t take because it has secured the floor space and the power. Customers co-invest in the capacity, which ties both sides to the same production lines. CLS is also automating rack assembly, cabling and fibre insertion, work that sits in the most labour-constrained part of the process.

The company acknowledges new bidders. It also says customers sometimes move older products elsewhere to free capacity for new ones.

Valuation: why the target moves to $560

The full model is here.

Keeping BUY. The target moves to $560 from $575, the first time I’ve cut it. It started at $153 in the April 2025 deep dive, then went to $253 and $320 in 2025, $416 in January and $575 days later, after the Q4 2025 print.

Revenue. The model takes the company’s numbers for the two years it has guided and haircuts the first year it hasn’t. 2028 grows 19% to $47.6B, below what the awarded-programme forecasts point to. Customer demand forecasts turn into revenue when the components, the power and the floor space exist to ship them, and all three are scarce. From there growth fades in a straight line to 2.5%, and the business ends 2036 five times this year’s size.

Margins. CCS goes from 8.8% this year to 10% in the long run on HPS mix, 1.6T and co-packaged optics, and ATS from 6.4% to 7%. The model’s 2027 company margin of 8.7% sits below the 9% guide, and the model counts stock-based compensation as a cost, so its EBIT margin runs below management’s adjusted operating margin every year.

Cash. Capex runs at 4.8% of revenue this year and 4.4% next year, against 1.6% in 2025, before settling at 3%. Inventory days stay high through the ramp and payables days come back down from today’s stretched level. That produces FCF of $0.55B this year, -$1.4B in 2027 and a return to positive cash in 2028, the same shape management guided.

Discount rate. WACC is 8.4%, against 8.5% in January. A higher risk-free rate, in line with a 10-year Treasury near 5%, is offset by a lower equity risk premium. Terminal growth comes down to 2.5% from 3%.

The revenue base went up far more than the value did. What pushed the value up: a 2026 that is 24% larger than the model carried in January, a 2027 that is 83% larger, and $3.1B of net cash. What pulled it down: the cash this ramp consumes before it pays, 11.1M more shares and a lower terminal growth rate. Net, the target moves 3% lower.

Two inputs carry most of the value. Every 5 points of 2028 CCS growth moves it $90-$110 a share, and every half point of long-term CCS margin moves it $29.

What $258 implies

Take the 2027 guide as given and keep the model’s margins and cash needs. For the shares to be worth $258, revenue has to slip in 2028 and then sit near $40B for nine years. That’s the world where hyperscalers and labs keep buying racks at the 2027 pace every year to 2036 and never spend a dollar more on them.

There are two other ways to get to $258. One keeps the model’s revenue and lets the long-term CCS margin fall below its 2022 level. The other keeps everything and demands a return near 13% a year.

The company has awarded programmes that make 2028 larger than 2027. Broadcom, whose silicon sits inside most of its programmes, has line of sight to doubling AI revenue again in 2028. Its two biggest new programmes ramp in the second half of 2027, which means 2028 gets a full year of them. And at $258 you pay 12x next year’s guided EPS for a company growing it 86%.

Mr. Market is pricing 2027 as the peak. I think 2027 is the year the voice in his head confuses a cash-hungry ramp with a business at its top.

Risk register

Customer concentration

The three largest customers made up 66% of Q3 revenue, against 59% a year ago, and the top ten 85%. In the April 2025 deep dive, the two largest were 28% and 11% of revenue. The sequential improvement I noted in July reversed. CLS is now more a bet on Google’s TPU programme than on hyperscaler capex in general, and a pause at the largest customer would put 35% of revenue at risk.

My answer: The concentration is the price of being inside the roadmaps that matter. These programmes run on design cycles of up to 24 months and span several generations, so a customer can’t swap CLS out between one quarter and the next. The 2027 ramps add OpenAI and the AMD Helios programmes at scale, which spreads the revenue across more names inside the same concentrated market. The risk stays live: a slowdown at the largest customer would hit revenue before any diversification shows up.

Who pays for the build

The labs are growing faster than their cash flows, and the vendors are financing the gap. By my count, Anthropic’s S-1 adds up to $780B-$810B of compute arrangements, about $430B of them non-cancelable or owed regardless of usage, and Broadcom will lend Anthropic up to $42B through convertible notes to pay the rent on its TPU racks. If funding for the labs dries up, orders slow, and CLS feels it with a lag equal to the length of its order book.

My answer: CLS doesn’t finance its customers. It buys long-lead components against non-cancellable orders, assesses each inventory build against the customer’s credit at the time, and asks for third-party funding support or contractual backstops where it needs them. The CFO said the company sees no financial distress across its customer base. The exposure is real and it arrives in 2028 or later, which is the year to watch rather than this one.

Working capital and trade credit

Inventory is $4.5B and rising, payables days stretched to 74, and 2027 consumes cash. If suppliers tighten terms in the middle of the ramp, the payables that funded this quarter’s inventory have to be paid in cash.

My answer: The balance sheet is built for this. $5.7B of liquidity covers the model’s 2027 cash burn four times, and $561M of customer deposits sit against the inventory. The August raise was expensive for existing holders, and it bought the room to absorb a supplier squeeze.

Execution and supply

2027 is weighted to the second half, and every large ramp in it depends on components, power and buildings arriving on time. Management named land, power and geopolitics as the constraints on beating the outlook.

My answer: CLS has cleared the top of its EPS range for five quarters through tight supply. The risk here is timing between quarters, and the model already haircuts 2028.

The value sits in the 2030s

77% of the model’s enterprise value is terminal value. The target depends on the business still growing at mid-single digits in 2035 and holding a 10% CCS margin.

My answer: That’s true of every growth company valued on cash flow, and it’s why I haircut 2028 and fade growth to 2.5%. At $258 you don’t need the 2030s to work. You need revenue to grow after 2027 at all.

Verdict

Keeping BUY. Target trimmed to $560 from $575.

The position stays at 6.8% of the portfolio.

In August, new shareholders paid $310 for a company that had told them 2027 would grow faster than 65%. Since then the 2027 revenue outlook came in 18% above that floor, the 2026 FCF outlook fell $140M, and the shares fell 17%. I’d make that exchange every time.

If this helped you see past the tape, share it with someone who owns CLS or is thinking about it.
